analysis.one_liner: Imposes new federal rules on payday and online small-dollar lenders to curb fees, fraud, and data harvesting.
analysis.headline: The SAFE Lending Act, which would have registered small-dollar lenders with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and barred many overdraft and lead-generation practices, never received a committee hearing or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted the payday and online small-dollar lending industry, where loans of a few hundred dollars often carry triple-digit annual interest rates. It would have required lenders making loans under $5,000 to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, forced online and bank-originated small-dollar loans to follow each state's interest-rate caps, banned overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, limited unsolicited 'remotely created checks' that let lenders pull money from bank accounts, and barred companies that collect borrowers' bank logins and Social Security numbers from selling that data unless they are the actual lender. It also ordered a study of small-dollar lending's effects in Indian Country. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who use payday, installment, and online small-dollar loans — disproportionately low-income households living paycheck to paycheck — gain protections against hidden fees, unauthorized bank withdrawals, unlicensed online lenders evading state rate caps, and lead-generation websites that harvest sensitive financial data and sell it to lenders. Consumers using prepaid accounts gain freedom from overdraft fees.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any person issuing small-dollar consumer credit (loans up to $5,000, payable within roughly a year) to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before making loans, and covers the brokers and lead generators that feed them customers.

Requires online, phone, mail, and national-bank small-dollar loans to comply with the interest-rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives, closing loopholes that let lenders charge rates a state has outlawed.

Extends Electronic Fund Transfer Act protections — including the right to stop payments — to one-time electronic debits used to collect small-dollar loan payments, treating them like preauthorized transfers.
Bars charging overdraft fees on prepaid accounts and lets the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau further restrict prepaid fees by rule.

Restricts the sale and distribution of sensitive personal financial information (Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, access codes) in connection with small-dollar loans to companies that are actually lending the money, and requires lead generators to disclose who they are.

Limits remotely created checks — payment orders created without the account holder's signature that have been a vehicle for unauthorized withdrawals — to parties the consumer has designated in writing, with a right to revoke the designation.

Directs the Government Accountability Office to study capital access on tribal reservations and the effects of small-dollar lending on tribal members' economic opportunity, with congressional committees to receive the results.

analysis.who_pays: Payday, installment, and online small-dollar lenders lose the ability to operate outside state rate caps and registration rules; lead-generation companies and data brokers lose the business of selling borrowers' financial information; banks that originate loans on payday lenders' behalf to evade state caps (rent-a-bank arrangements) face new state-law compliance; prepaid card programs lose overdraft fee revenue.

drawbacks.text: Applying state interest-rate caps to online and bank-originated small-dollar loans could shrink the supply of legal short-term credit, leaving some borrowers with no option but informal lenders, bounced checks, or utility shut-offs if no adequate alternatives exist.

The registration requirement and lead-generation ban add compliance burdens on any facilitator of small-dollar loans, which could push smaller or tribal-affiliated lenders out of the market while established firms absorb the costs.
The bill relies heavily on Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rulemaking within one year, so its real-world effect would have depended on how the Bureau chose to implement it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the protections are concrete and targeted at documented industry practices: unauthorized remotely created checks, data harvesting by lead generators, and loans structured to evade state rate caps. The main honest trade-off is that restricting high-cost credit without simultaneously expanding cheaper alternatives can reduce credit access for the riskiest borrowers; the bill's mandated study of small-dollar lending in tribal communities acknowledged the availability-of-credit side of the question but did not itself create alternatives. On balance the design addresses the fraud and evasion problem rather than banning the product outright.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on February 13, 2018, joined by 11 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
The bill gathered 19 cosponsors, all Democrats, but its only action after introduction was the committee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and unreported bills expire when a Congress ends; the bill would have needed to be reintroduced to move in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, online installment, and tribal-affiliated lenders, lead-generation data brokers, and banks in rent-a-bank partnerships kept operating under the pre-existing rules, free of the registration requirement, state rate-cap compliance mandate, and lead-generation restrictions the bill would have imposed. Borrowers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFE Lending Act and led it as sole sponsor.

for.name: Rep. Elijah Cummings
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at introduction.

for.name: 19 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every recorded cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: The Financial Services Committee, which he chaired, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without any action after its referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican support is recorded; the committee chaired by a Republican never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill would have required registration with the CFPB and forced online and bank-originated loans to obey state interest-rate caps, directly threatening the triple-digit-rate business model these lenders use in states that have banned or capped it. Borrowers would have paid less and faced fewer unauthorized withdrawals.

industries.industry: Lead generators and consumer-data brokers in consumer credit
industries.note: The bill bars companies from distributing borrowers' Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and account access codes in connection with small-dollar loans unless they are the actual lender, eliminating a data-harvesting business that runs on people's most sensitive financial information.

industries.industry: Banks in rent-a-bank partnerships with high-cost lenders
industries.note: By applying state rate laws to small-dollar loans 'conducted by a national bank,' the bill would have closed the arrangement where a partner bank originates a loan on a payday lender's behalf to import the bank's preemption from state rate caps.

industries.industry: Prepaid card issuers and program managers
industries.note: The bill bans charging overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, a fee stream paid disproportionately by consumers using prepaid cards in place of bank accounts.

industries.industry: Lenders and businesses operating on tribal reservations
industries.note: The bill orders a Government Accountability Office study of capital availability on reservations and the effects of small-dollar lending on tribal members, rather than singling out tribal lenders for regulation; the study itself imposes no cost, and the bill's provisions would apply to online tribal lending only through the general state-law compliance mandate.
